messages.subject: Comparing Observers Detectability Curve
messages.body_plain:
Hello=2C

What is the most widely accepted statistical method for comparing detectabi=
lity curves between observers? I want to say with some degree of confidence=
 (90% or 95%) that observers detection curves for a particular organism are=
 different.

Thanks=2C

Tyler

messages.subject: Re: Comparing Observers Detectability Curve
messages.body_plain:
On 11/11/2010 16:22, Tyler Hicks wrote:
> > Hello,
> >
> > What is the most widely accepted statistical method for comparing detectability curves between observers? I want to say with some degree of confidence (90% or 95%) that observers detection curves for a particular organism are different.
That would be confusing confidence intervals with hypothesis testing.

You could fit a single model to the pooled data from observers, and
include observer as a factor-type covariate using the mcds engine.  Then
fit the same model, without observer.  AIC would allow you to assess
whether you need to allow for different detection functions by observer.

If you have more than 2 observers and want pairwise tests, then you
could group distances by observer and by distance interval, and do
chi-square contingency table tests for each observer pair.  In fact, you
could do a single test in this way:  if you have r observers and c
distance intervals, you can create an r by c contingency table.  Each of
the r times c entries will be the number of detections made by a given
observer in a given distance interval.

If your chi-square statistic is significant at say the 5% level, you
would conclude that there is evidence that the observers' detection
functions differ.

Steve Buckland
--

Hello all

apply a tweedie distribution to the data by running the model in R direct=
ly - as this type of distribution is not offered in Distance yet.

I have managed to get the code to work all the way through to the varianc=
e code which does not appear to be running.

2,link=3D"log"),data=3Ddata2,method=3D"REML")

messages.subject: Free Statistics Learning & Teaching Resources
messages.body_plain:
APOLOGIES FOR CROSS-POSTING

List members may be interested in the free Statistics teaching and learning
resources on our website at:

http://www.conceptstew.co.uk/PAGES/freeresources2.html.

As well as a plain-english glossary of statistical terms, we have a series
of discussion pieces about different aspects of statistical thinking which
people often find confusing. Where possible we use real-life examples to
illustrate these.

Concepts covered so far include decision-making and the nature of risk,
conditional probability, when to use the mean or the median, clinical
trials, the prosecutor's fallacy, sample size, etc. The next item scheduled
will be on reporting confidence intervals. We add new pieces regularly and
would be like to hear from anyone with suggestions of what we should cover.

You are welcome to use these in your own teaching or learning, and please
feel free to forward this email to anyone who might be interested.

Kind regards,

Jill
